note.text:
Geography is the study of the Earth’s surface: its land, water, air, plants and animals, the people who live on it, and how people and their surroundings affect each other.
Branches:
• Physical geography: landforms, rivers, climate, soils, vegetation.
• Human geography: population, settlements, farming, industry, trade, transport.
• Practical geography: map reading, fieldwork, graphs and statistics.
Sub-branches include climatology (climate), geomorphology (landforms), hydrology (water), pedology (soils), biogeography, population, settlement, economic and transport geography, and cartography (making maps).
Methods: observation, interviews, questionnaires, measurement, maps and photographs.
Why study it? To understand and protect our environment, to plan farms and towns, to read maps and find our way, and for jobs such as surveyor, weather forecaster and town planner.

worked_example.problem: A class visits the Wouri River in Douala. They measure how fast the water flows, and they ask fishermen how much fish they catch. Which branches of geography are they using?
steps: How fast a river flows is about water: physical geography (hydrology).
Fishing as a way of earning a living is human geography (economic geography).
Measuring and asking questions outside the classroom is fieldwork: practical geography.
worked_example.answer: Physical, human and practical geography together.

cards.idea: Geography studies the Earth’s surface and the people on it, and how people and their surroundings affect each other.
example: Why does Buea get more rain than Maroua? Why do people build towns beside rivers? These are geography questions.

check.prompt: Which question is a geography question?

right.text: Why do many people live near the coast?
Why does the north of Cameroon get less rain than the south?
Where are the main roads in Cameroon?

wrong.text: What is the past tense of “go”?
How does the heart pump blood?
Who was the first president of Cameroon?

cards.idea: Geography has three branches: physical geography (the natural world), human geography (people and what they do) and practical geography (maps and fieldwork).
example: Hills and rivers: physical. Markets and roads: human. Drawing a map of the school: practical.

cards.idea: Each branch has sub-branches: climatology studies climate, pedology studies soils, cartography is making maps.
example: A weather forecaster uses climatology. A map maker uses cartography.

questions.prompt: Which is a good reason to study geography?

right.text: It helps us understand and protect our environment.
It helps farmers plan their work with the seasons.
It helps us read maps and find our way.
It helps planners decide where to build roads and schools.

wrong.text: It teaches doctors how to cure diseases.
It is only about learning the names of capital cities.
wrong.explain: Geography studies the land, the weather and people, not just names.

wrong.text: It tells us exactly what will happen in the future.
wrong.explain: Geography helps us plan, but it cannot tell the future exactly.

wrong.text: It is only useful for pilots.
wrong.explain: Everyone uses geography: farmers, traders, travellers, planners.

questions.prompt: One sentence is wrong. Which one?

right.text: Hydrology is the study of water.
Pedology is the study of soils.
Cartography is the making of maps.
Human geography studies people and their activities.
Climatology is the study of climate.

wrong.text: Geomorphology is the study of population.
wrong.explain: Geomorphology studies landforms; population is studied in population geography.

wrong.text: Physical geography studies towns and markets.
wrong.explain: Towns and markets are human geography.

wrong.text: A questionnaire is watching people without asking them anything.
wrong.explain: That is observation; a questionnaire is a list of written questions.
